sentences: You are standing in front of the Diwan-i-Aam, the hall of public audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648 and held his first court here soon after.
It is built entirely of red sandstone, and it was once covered in gilding and painted plaster, all of which is gone.
Inside, four columns carry each arch, in seven bays across three aisles.
In the middle of the far wall there is a recess raised above the floor.
That is where the Emperor sat.
The lawn in front of you stands in for a courtyard that ran five hundred and sixty feet.
The shrubberies mark where the arcades used to be, and every morning they were full of men waiting to be seen.
This is the Rang Mahal, the painted palace.
It is named for the colour that once covered the inside of these walls, and almost none of it is left.
Shah Jahan knew it as the Imtiyaz Mahal, the palace of distinction, and it was the largest apartment in the imperial household.
A marble channel runs the length of the floor, and at its centre sits a basin cut from a single block of Makrana marble.
The ceiling was silver first, then copper, then wood.
Each replacement was a smaller claim than the one before.
Behind you, between this hall and the back of the Diwan-i-Aam, there was a walled garden with a tank at its centre.
It lay buried until 1911, when it was uncovered again.
This is the Diwan-i-Khas, the hall of private audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648, and a nineteenth century surveyor called it the most highly ornamented building he ever put up.
Look at the lower part of the piers.
Every piece of coloured stone in them was cut to fit a socket chiselled out of the marble.
Higher up, the arches were gilded and painted.
The marble channel running down the centre of the floor was called the Nahr-i-Bihisht, the stream of paradise.
The peacock throne stood on the dais in this room until 1739, when Nadir Shah carried it away to Persia.
He accepted the surrender of the Mughal Emperor here first, and took the throne afterwards.
